How to Plan a Website Project: Goals, Sitemap and Content Before Design

Most website delays come from decisions made too late. Plan goals, pages and content first, and the design and build go far more smoothly.

VXVintorex Digital team3 min read · Evergreen guide

Key takeaways

  • Write down the one or two outcomes the website must achieve before anything else.
  • A sitemap agreed early prevents scope creep and surprise costs.
  • Content is usually the slowest part, so start gathering it on day one.
  • Agree on review rounds and a single decision-maker to keep approvals moving.

Define the goal in one sentence

“We want more enquiries for our three main services from customers in our city” is a goal. “We need a modern website” is not. A clear goal decides what goes on the home page, which pages exist and what you measure after launch.

Know your audience

List the two or three types of people who visit your site and what each needs. A first-time customer wants reassurance and pricing guidance. A returning client wants contact details and support. A job seeker wants your careers page. Design the navigation around these needs, not your internal departments.

Build the sitemap

A sitemap is the list of pages and how they connect. Keep it simple:

  1. Home
  2. About
  3. Services, with one page per service
  4. Projects or case studies
  5. Blog or resources (optional)
  6. Contact
  7. Privacy policy and terms

Agree on the sitemap with your web team before design starts. Adding pages later is possible, but it usually costs time and money.

Gather content early

Content, not code, is the most common reason websites launch late.
  • Text: write or commission copy for each page. Short paragraphs, clear headings, plain language.
  • Photos: real photos of your team, premises and work build more trust than stock images.
  • Logos and brand files: high-resolution logo files, colours and fonts.
  • Proof: testimonials, client names you have permission to use, certifications.
  • Legal: privacy policy, terms and refund policy if you sell online.

Look at references together

Collect three to five websites you like and note exactly what you like about each: the layout, the tone, the way services are presented. Collect a couple you dislike too. This gives designers direction far faster than adjectives like “clean” or “bold”.

Agree on the process

  • One person on your side gives consolidated feedback and final approvals.
  • A fixed number of revision rounds is agreed upfront.
  • Feedback is specific: “move the phone number above the fold”, not “make it pop”.
  • Each stage, from wireframes to design, build and launch, is signed off before the next begins.

Plan the launch and what comes after

Before launch, test every form, link and page on mobile and desktop. Set up redirects if you are replacing an old site so existing search rankings and bookmarks keep working. After launch, decide who updates content, who handles backups and security, and how you will review results each month.

Frequently asked questions

How long does a typical business website take?

A small site can be ready in one to three weeks once content is available. Larger or custom sites take longer. The biggest variable is usually how quickly content and approvals arrive.

What happens to my old website’s search rankings?

Rankings carry over best when old page addresses are redirected to their new equivalents and important content is kept. Plan redirects before launch, not after.
